newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe urged to act on high spending deficit.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe urged to act on high spending deficit.

text.p: Captains of Zimbabwean industries urged the government on Friday to use its next budget to whittle down its high spending deficit threatening economic growth.

Closing a congress of the Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries (CZI) in the northern resort town of Victoria Falls, CZI president Jonee Blanchfield warned of economic stagnation if the current environment of high inflation and interest rates continued.

"The time has now come for us...to acknowledge that we can no longer postpone action to whittle down the deficit. The havoc caused on the economy by the deficit -- the highest in Africa and in much of the world -- has been enormous," she said.

She said the deficit was frightening away foreign investors from the southern African state and forcing the government to rely on the local money market for funds, denying the private sector vital money for expansion and growth. Lack of sustainable growth has left unemployment at around 50 percent in the formal sector.

"It is now up to us to use the coming national budget as a turning point, a point when we acknowledge our mistakes and take bold corrective action," she said of Zimbabwe's 1997/98 budget due to be presented on July 24.

"We are extremely adept at identifying problems and suggesting right solutions. But we procrastinate! It is time we boldly took decisions...so that we can act. Only by acting with urgency will we achieve real prosperity now," she added.
President Robert Mugabe's government has failed since it launchad market economic reforms in 1991, to meet deficit-reduction targets.
In 1995, this led the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, which backed Zimbabwe's first five-year reform programme, to withhold some crucial balance-of-payments support.
The donors say they are now looking to the country's new budget -- which will run for 18 months from this month to December 1998 -- before deciding on when to resume aid for more reforms.

In an interview with Reuters on Thursday, Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa forecast the budget deficit for the 1996/97 fiscal year ended June 30 at 10.3 percent of gross domestic product, lower than earlier predictions of about 11 percent of GDP but still off a target of 8.5 percent.
